craft_claim: Controlling, high-threat language raises reactance in the form of anger and counterarguing, and sustained moral absolutism lowers tolerance of dissenters, so high-intensity defiance must be dosed and must yield at stakes peaks.

supporting_evidence.note: Dillard and Shen show reactance is intertwined cognition and affect, measurable by self-report and linked to anger directed at the message source; controlling language and threats raise it and increase counterarguing.

supporting_evidence.location: Psychological Reactance: A Theory of Freedom and Control, ch. 2
supporting_evidence.note: Reactance magnitude grows with the importance and proportion of freedoms threatened, so piling on threats compounds resistance rather than persuasion.

supporting_evidence.location: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 88(6):895-917
supporting_evidence.note: Moral mandates predict greater preferred distance from attitudinally dissimilar others, so holding a reader in sustained absolutism narrows the audience the text can reach.
Enduring empowerment depends on action expressing social identity, so repetition without an articulated 'we' produces slogans rather than empowerment, an argument for dosing the register.

counterevidence.note: Anger is itself a mobilizer when joined to efficacy and identity, so the dosage concern is excess intensity without those terms, not anger as such.

scope: Long-form, serial, and persuasion-of-undecided content across all forms.
exceptions: Very short forms (epigram, chant, poem) may legitimately hold a single high-intensity note; the dosage findings concern sustained prose.
